about: The Greater Doxology, the angelic hymn: it opens with the angels' song over Bethlehem (Lk 2:14 — the Vulgate there has “in altíssimis”, the hymn sings “in excélsis”) and unfolds into an early Christian hymn of praise, originally sung in Greek at the morning prayer of the East and translated into Latin in antiquity. By an old Roman tradition it was first heard at Mass in the night of Christmas; for centuries it was reserved to bishops' Masses, priests being allowed to intone it only at Easter — a restriction that vanished toward the end of the eleventh century.

s01.narrative: At the middle of the altar the priest intones the angelic hymn — the song the angels sang over Bethlehem (Lk 2:14). At High Mass all stand at the intonation. The rubric has it said “si dicendum est” — if it falls to be said: it is omitted, among other days, at the seasonal Masses of Advent, Pre-Lent and Lent and at Requiem Masses, and returns on the feasts of those seasons. At the words “Adorámus te”, “Grátias ágimus tibi”, “Jesu Christe” and “Súscipe deprecatiónem” the priest bows his head, and at “Cum Sancto Spíritu” he signs himself with the cross.

s02.translation: Glory to God in the highest.

s03.translation: And on earth peace to men of good will.

s04.translation: We praise you. We bless you. We adore you. We glorify you.

s05.translation: We give you thanks for your great glory.

s06.translation: Lord God, heavenly King, God the Father almighty.

s08.translation: Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father.

s09.translation: You who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.

s10.translation: You who take away the sins of the world, receive our plea.

s11.translation: You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us.

s12.translation: For you alone are the Holy One. You alone are the Lord. You alone are the Most High, Jesus Christ.

s13.translation: With the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.

w001.function: A sentence with no verb — supply “let there be”: glory (be) to God. To whom? — that is the dative “Deo” (w004).

w003.function: An adjective doing a noun's work: “the highest (places)”.

w011.function: Genitive of quality: men “of good will” — together with “bonæ” (w010) it says what kind of men the peace is promised to.

w021.function: Literally “we do” — the object is “Grátias” (w020), fronted for emphasis.

w028.function: The form looks like a nominative but is an address here — like the neighboring “Dómine” (w027).

w035.function: A true vocative of “fílius” — the -i ending. Compare “Fílius” (w043), where the same person is named with the nominative form.

w041.function: Apposition to “Dómine” (w039) — a nominative form serving as an address. Latin often does this in long apostrophes; the vocative proper would be “agne”.

w043.function: Again a nominative serving as an address — right after the true vocative “Fili” (w035) the hymn shows both of Latin's options.

w045.function: The relative refers to “you” — which is why the verb “tollis” (w046) stands in the second person: “(you,) who take away”.

w049.function: It looks passive but means actively — the plea “have mercy”. Here with the dative “nobis” (w050); in the psalms the same verb takes the genitive (miserére mei).

w055.function: An imperative — the hymn's petition addressed directly to the Lamb; its object is “deprecatiónem” (w056).

w061.function: The preposition “ad” with the accusative marks place here, not motion — the same fixed phrase as the Creed's “sedet ad déxteram Patris”.

w067.function: “You alone” — in Latin an adjective beside the pronoun, with no verb: an implied “es” (are) must be supplied in all three sentences of this verse.

w068.function: An adjective doing a title's work: “the Holy One” as a name of God — as in “Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus”.

w074.function: Like “Sanctus” (w068) — an adjective serving as a predicate title; the peak of the three-step ladder: Holy One, Lord, Most High.

w077.function: “Cum” with the ablative — “with the Holy Spirit”: the hymn's whole ending is Trinitarian, like the lesser doxology.
